digest.top_line: ASCO advanced prostate imaging guideline: NGI should be offered for rising PSA post-RP when salvage RT is contemplated (rec 4.4), its sole high-quality, strong recommendation.
digest.tldr: Guidance-heavy day: four consensus documents and a case-based guide, no new trial data. Prostate carried most: ASCO ties next-generation imaging to a live salvage decision, and the ESTRO ACROP Delphi reached consensus on only 14/40 items (35%) for intraprostatic salvage SBRT, leaving dose and fractionation divided. Gyn adds ABS HDR schedules with EQD2 goals and ESGO/ESTRO/ESP universal MMR/MSI testing.

sites.intro: All guidance, no trials: imaging selection before salvage, salvage SBRT for intraprostatic relapse after RT, and a 40 Gy/5fx primary SBRT worked example.

studies.name: Radiosurgery Society SBRT guide for localized prostate cancer
studies.tldr: 40 Gy/5fx to prostate + proximal 1cm SV as worked example; large gland and poor baseline IPSS framed as counselling issues, not SBRT contraindications.
details: 🔍 Case-based guide endorsed by the Radiosurgery Society (Pract Radiat Oncol 2024); two modified real-world cases, not a trial
🔍 Scope: dose/fractionation, OAR constraints, dose escalation, rectal spacer, ADT with SBRT, high-risk, large prostate, IBD, MRI guidance

details.text: 💊 Case A: 78yo, unfavorable intermediate-risk, cT1cN0M0, PSA 8.1, 112 mL gland on MRI
subdetails: Leuprolide started 2 mo pre-SBRT; gland 61 mL on pre-SBRT MRI; 6 mo ADT total
40Gy/5fx to 100% isodose covering PTV, V105% (42 Gy) < 20-30%
Acute GU flare managed with doubled tamsulosin + ibuprofen; IPSS 10 at 1 yr

details: 💊 Case B: MRI-guided SBRT, 40 Gy/5fx with SIB 42 Gy/5fx to dominant intraprostatic lesion, hip prosthesis
📐 Prescription practice varies: 100% isodose covering 95-99% of target vs robotic 75-85% isodose (Dmax 130-140%)
🔗 PACE-B: only 5% of pts had prostate volume ≥80 mL, so large-gland SBRT data are thin
📊 Large glands: one retrospective series flagged ≥50 mL as predictor of late G2+ GU toxicity; others show favorable toxicity at ≥50-100 mL
📊 Baseline IPSS ≥15 with prophylactic α1-antagonists: low G3 GU rates in retrospective series
⚠️ Guide advises against neoadjuvant ADT solely for cytoreduction, yet Case A received it (for UIR disease)
⚠️ Large-gland, high-IPSS and prior-TURP guidance rests on retrospective series and extrapolation
⚠️ Excerpt truncated: Case 2 discussion, spacer, ADT and dose-escalation sections not in source text
studies.significance: The planning detail is the transferable part: 40 Gy prescribed to the 100% isodose covering PTV with V105% (42 Gy) held under 20-30%, versus robotic practice at the 75-85% isodose. Large glands and baseline IPSS ≥15 are treated as counselling and prophylaxis problems, since PACE-B enrolled only 5% of pts at ≥80 mL.
studies.monday_clinic: In localized prostate cancer with a large gland, high baseline IPSS or prior TURP, this guide supports offering SBRT when OAR constraints are achievable, with explicit counselling on transient obstructive flare; it does not support ADT given solely for gland cytoreduction.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Worked example is **40 Gy in 5 fractions** to prostate + proximal 1cm SV, every other day, VMAT with hydrogel spacer. MRI-guided case adds a **42 Gy SIB** to the dominant intraprostatic lesion.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: PACE-B underpins SBRT as standard, but only **5%** of its pts had glands ≥80 mL; the authors look to PACE-B subgroup analyses and the MIRAGE randomized trial (MRI guidance) for toxicity questions the guide cannot settle.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intact-prostate localized disease, including large glands, poor baseline urinary function and prior TURP. Does not represent post-prostatectomy or nodal/pelvic SBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Whether the larger GU flare in big glands is **specific to SBRT fractionation** or generic to any RT remains open. Prior-TURP data are mixed, so the guide recommends counselling rather than exclusion.

studies.interpretation:
This is a practice guide, not evidence generation, and its value lies in how it handles the gap between what the randomized data tested and who actually walks into an SBRT clinic. PACE-B established ultrahypofractionation as standard for intact prostate disease, but the guide is candid that the trial population skews away from the hard cases: only 5% of PACE-B pts had glands of 80 mL or more. Everything the authors say about large glands, poor baseline urinary function and prior TURP is therefore extrapolation from retrospective series, and a reader should weigh it as reasoned expert opinion rather than tested policy.

The large-gland argument is the most consequential. The authors concede that conventionally fractionated, moderately hypofractionated and brachytherapy series all show more GU toxicity in bigger glands, and that one SBRT series identified 50 mL as an independent predictor of late grade 2+ GU toxicity. They then lean on other series showing acceptable toxicity at 50 to 100 mL and conclude that gland size alone should not exclude SBRT if constraints are met. That conclusion is defensible but not proven, and the authors themselves name the unresolved question: whether the flare is worse with SBRT-type fractionation or simply a feature of prostate RT in a big gland. Until PACE-B subgroup data or prospective large-gland cohorts answer it, the honest position is the one they land on, namely informed counselling plus prophylactic α1-antagonists or anti-inflammatories.

There is an internal tension worth noticing. The text advises against neoadjuvant ADT purely for cytoreduction, yet the illustrative Case A received leuprolide before SBRT and the gland shrank from 112 to 61 mL. The ADT there is justified by unfavorable intermediate-risk disease, but a reader could easily take the case as tacit endorsement of downsizing. The distinction matters for a 78-year-old with cardiac disease and diabetes, where ADT toxicity is not trivial.

The planning section is the most transferable content. Making explicit that some centres prescribe to the 100% isodose with tight hot-spot limits while robotic users prescribe to a lower isodose with much higher maximum dose is useful, because published SBRT outcomes are not dose-equivalent across these conventions even at the same nominal prescription. Readers comparing their own results to trial data should know which convention generated those data.

The excerpt available here is truncated before the second case discussion and the sections on spacer, ADT and dose escalation, so judgments on those topics cannot be made from this source.

Large glands and baseline IPSS ≥15 are treated as counselling and prophylaxis problems, since PACE-B enrolled only 5% of pts at ≥80 mL.

studies.name: ESTRO ACROP Delphi: salvage SBRT for intraprostatic relapse
studies.tldr: Consensus on 14/40 items (35%) for intraprostatic relapse after RT: focal GTV-based CTV, no concurrent ADT; dose, fractionation, OAR limits unresolved.
details: 🔍 3-round Delphi, Jul 22 to Dec 16, 2019; 40 questions across 3 sections
🔍 Panel: 18 of 33 contacted salvage SBRT authors (54.5%); all completed every round
🔍 Consensus defined as >80% agreement; major agreement 65-80%; divided <65%
📊 Consensus on 14/40 (35%); consensus or major agreement on 27/40 (68%)

rows: Primary RT dose informs salvage dose
Minimum interval from primary RT: 2 yr
Max T, Gleason, PSA for selection

details: ⚠️ Discussion cites a 5-6 fx schedule to ~35 Gy, yet results list fractionation as divided
⚠️ Rounds closed before most PSMA-PET detection data were published; dated imaging section
⚠️ Only 2 respondents outside Europe (both US); 12/18 (67%) at centres treating >2,000 pts/yr
🔗 vs Uro-GEC-ESTRO salvage BT Delphi: that panel split on target volume; this one agreed on focal GTV-based CTV

verdict.rationale: Expert Delphi of 18 salvage SBRT authors; output is agreement, not outcomes. Dosimetry section weakest (Kendall's W 0.12), so dose guidance is absent.
verdict.audience: Intraprostatic relapse after primary prostate RT, metastases excluded

studies.significance: The panel converged on the target, not the dose: CTV = mpMRI GTV plus an adaptive margin, prescribed to an isodose. Salvage dose relative to primary, fractionation and cumulative OAR constraints stayed unresolved (dosimetry Kendall's W 0.12), so a re-RT prescription still has to come from the retrospective series and Pasquier's ongoing dose-finding phase I/II.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with intraprostatic relapse at least 2 yr after primary RT, metastases excluded, ECOG 0-1, prior ADT allowed, this supports focal salvage SBRT without concurrent ADT as an expert-endorsed way to defer ADT; it does not settle eligibility after prior G2 late toxicity, where the panel split.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **ESTRO ACROP Delphi**, 3 rounds run Jul 22 to Dec 16, 2019, **40 questions** in 3 sections (patient selection, imaging/biopsy, dosimetry). **Consensus = >80% agreement**, major agreement 65-80%, divided <65%. An item that reached consensus was dropped from later rounds.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Panel was **18 of 33** contacted authors of salvage SBRT papers (54.5%), and all completed every round. Only 2 practised outside Europe (both US), and **12/18 (67%)** worked at centres treating >2,000 pts/yr. The questionnaire was reviewed by a committee that included an EAU-nominated urologist.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Consensus: **CTV = mpMRI GTV + adaptive margin**, primary RT dose factored into the salvage dose, **no concomitant ADT**, Phoenix definition for follow-up. Major agreement: prescribe to the isodose, **2 yr minimum** from primary RT. **Divided:** salvage dose vs primary, fractionation, cumulative OAR constraints.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Consensus on 14/40 (35%)**, half of it reached in round 1 (7/14). Consensus or major agreement on 27/40 (68%).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The Uro-GEC-ESTRO salvage brachytherapy Delphi (Kaljouw) split on target volume and required histology. This panel agreed on a **focal GTV-based CTV** but split on biopsy. Italian AIRO PROLAPSE respondents leaned toward concurrent ADT, which this panel rejected, and the MASTER meta-analysis (150 studies) found no significant 5-yr RFS difference between salvage RP and other local modalities.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with intraprostatic relapse after primary prostate RT, metastatic disease excluded, ECOG 0-1. Does not represent nodal or distant relapse, post-RP prostate-bed relapse, or a choice between SBRT and salvage RP, HDR BT or ADT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The panel came from salvage SBRT authors, so nobody tested whether the modality itself is right. Rounds closed before most PSMA-PET detection data were published, which likely explains **PSMA-PET at 28%** vs choline PET at 89%. The discussion cites a 5-6 fx schedule to ~35 Gy while the results list fractionation as divided.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The panel agreed on selection and target logic and **split on everything that needs outcome data**: dose, fractionation, OAR limits, biopsy. Ongoing protocols diverge on the same points: Bergamin requires a 4-yr interval where Pasquier and Fuller use 2 yr, and Fuller treats the whole gland where the others treat part of it.

studies.interpretation:
Read this document as a map of where salvage SBRT practice had converged by late 2019, and where it had not, drawn by the people who wrote the retrospective series. Its value lies in where agreement fell, not in any single item. The panel converged on questions that can be answered from first principles or imaging logic: exclude metastases first, treat a focal mpMRI-defined target rather than the whole gland, keep ADT out of the re-irradiation course, and wait at least 2 years after the first course. It did not converge on anything that needs outcome data to settle: the salvage dose relative to the primary, the fractionation, and cumulative constraints for rectum, bladder, femoral heads and penile bulb. That split is itself the finding. The dosimetry section had the weakest concordance of the three, which tells a radiation oncologist that a re-irradiation prescription is still an institutional choice.

The target-volume result is the clearest change from the Uro-GEC-ESTRO brachytherapy Delphi. That panel split between whole-gland, partial and focal treatment, and this one agreed on a GTV plus adaptive margin. The Corkum systematic review, which found no local control or bRFS gain from whole-prostate re-RT and less severe late toxicity with partial re-RT, gives the focal position some outcome footing, though it pools retrospective data. The biopsy question runs the other way. The brachytherapy panel and current guidelines required histology, while this panel and the Italian AIRO survey split on whether imaging is enough. On ADT, the Italian respondents leaned toward concurrent use, so the ESTRO position against it is a real divergence, not a restatement.

The method should limit how much weight any single item carries. The panel was drawn from authors of salvage SBRT papers, a group already committed to the modality. Nobody was asked whether SBRT should be preferred over salvage prostatectomy, HDR brachytherapy or ADT, and the document cannot answer that. Only 2 respondents practised outside Europe, and 12 of 18 worked at very high-volume centres. The authors say the questions came mainly from clinical experience because the literature was thin, so consensus here measures shared habit as much as evidence. Imaging is the most dated section. The rounds closed before most PSMA-PET detection data appeared, which explains choline PET winning broad support while PSMA-PET drew 28%. A panel convened now would likely answer that item differently, and the biopsy question with it.

There is also an internal tension. The results describe fractionation as unresolved, while the discussion describes agreement on a 5-6 fraction schedule to about 35 Gy. The defensible reading is that hypofractionated SBRT in that range was common practice among the panellists, not a consensus recommendation.

The document is more useful for trial design than for an individual decision. The protocols it surveys disagree on exactly the points the panel left open. Bergamin required a longer interval from primary RT than Pasquier and Fuller, and Fuller treated the whole gland where the others treated part of it. The dose-finding phase I/II by Pasquier and colleagues is the study built to answer the question this consensus could not.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The panel converged on the target, not the dose: a focal mpMRI GTV plus adaptive margin, prescribed to an isodose, with no concurrent ADT. Salvage dose, fractionation and cumulative OAR constraints had no consensus (dosimetry Kendall's W 0.12), so re-RT dosing still rests on retrospective series and the ongoing dose-finding phase I/II.

studies.name: ASCO guideline: imaging for advanced prostate cancer
studies.tldr: NGI offered only when salvage or a change in care is live. 4.4 (salvage RT contemplated after RP) is the sole high-quality, strong recommendation.
details: 🔍 ASCO expert panel with SAR, ACR, SNMMI, AUA, ASTRO, SUO; systematic review 2013 to August 2018
🔍 Evidence base: 35 studies (17 systematic reviews, 18 primary research articles)
🔍 NGI defined: PSMA (where available), 11C-choline or 18F-fluciclovine PET/CT, PET/MRI, whole-body MRI, 18F-NaF PET/CT

details.text: 🧭 NGI recommendation by clinical scenario (negative conventional imaging unless stated)

rows: Rising PSA post-RP, not salvage candidate or unwilling
Rising PSA post-RP, salvage RT contemplated
Rising PSA post-RT, salvage not planned
Should not be offered, except IRB trial
Rising PSA post-RT, salvage local/regional therapy contemplated
Only if change in care contemplated
Conventional imaging; PSA alone not reason to change therapy
Could be contemplated, especially in a trial

details: 📊 Habl: 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT changed the RT plan in 59%, staging in 43%
📊 Albisinni: 76% (99 of 131) had a treatment plan change from 68Ga results
📊 Pooled 68Ga-PSMA detection: 50% at PSA <0.5 vs 95% at PSA >2 ng/mL
⚠️ Support is mostly detection and management change, not outcome after NGI-directed therapy
⚠️ Search closed August 2018, before randomized imaging-guided salvage RT data
⚠️ Recommendations for suspected high-risk / initial staging not in source excerpt
studies.significance: Only one recommendation is graded high quality and strong: NGI when salvage RT is contemplated after RP (4.4). The same post-RP scenario without salvage candidacy gets 'should not be offered' (4.3). Supporting data are management shifts (Habl: RT plan changed in 59%), so NGI earns its place by redrawing the salvage field, not by finding untreatable disease.
studies.monday_clinic: In a man with rising PSA after prostatectomy, negative conventional imaging and a salvage RT plan, this supports NGI before treatment planning; it does not extend to men who are not salvage candidates, where the guideline advises against NGI.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **ASCO guideline** from an expert panel with SAR, ACR, SNMMI, AUA, ASTRO and SUO. Systematic review of literature from **2013 to August 2018**. Recommendations typed as evidence-based, informal consensus or consensus.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men with advanced prostate cancer: newly diagnosed high-risk, suspected or confirmed metastatic, recurrent, or progressive on treatment. Evidence base **35 studies**: 17 systematic reviews and 18 primary research articles.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Only **4.4** (salvage RT contemplated after RP) is graded **high quality, strong**. NGI in mCRPC with suspected subclinical mets (4.10) rests on **insufficient** evidence, weak strength.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The search predates proPSMA (PSMA PET/CT vs conventional imaging for high-risk staging) and EMPIRE-1 (fluciclovine-guided vs conventional-imaging-guided salvage RT). Both tested with randomization questions this guideline grades on detection and management-change data.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with advanced prostate cancer whose local, regional or systemic management could change on NGI. Does not represent men with no salvage or care-change option, where NGI is advised against.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: NGI is a pooled category: PSMA, choline, fluciclovine, PET/MRI, whole-body MRI and 18F-NaF are listed as **interchangeable options**. The evidence tables mix tracers, PSA strata and reference standards.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The organizing rule is **image only when the answer can change treatment**. 4.7 applies it to hormone-sensitive metastatic disease, where NGI may shift intent away from oligometastatic multimodality therapy. The guideline flags this stage-migration consequence but, citing limited prospective data, cannot size it.

studies.interpretation:
This guideline's structure is more useful than any single recommendation in it: it ties imaging intensity to whether the result could change treatment. Next-generation imaging is endorsed where a local or regional salvage decision is live (4.4 after prostatectomy, 4.6 after RT) and withheld where it is not (4.3, 4.5). For a radiation oncologist that position holds together. The scan's value lies in redrawing a salvage field, or in steering a pt away from one that cannot succeed, not in finding disease nobody will treat.

The weakness is the kind of evidence behind it. The strongest recommendation, 4.4, is graded high quality and strong, yet the evidence tables support it mostly with detection rates, pooled sensitivity and specificity, and change-in-management proportions. Habl reported a changed RT plan in 59% and a stage change in 43% after 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT. Albisinni reported a changed plan in 76% (99 of 131). Those figures show the scan moves decisions. They do not show the moved decisions are better, and a management-change endpoint cannot tell a correct field extension apart from treatment of a false-positive node. The panel concedes the point in 4.5, which states there is little evidence that NGI alters treatment or prognosis in men with no salvage plan.

The search closed in August 2018, before prospective PSMA-PET accuracy data and before randomized evidence on imaging-guided salvage RT. proPSMA later compared PSMA PET/CT with conventional imaging for high-risk staging, and EMPIRE-1 randomized fluciclovine-guided against conventional-imaging-guided salvage RT. Both test the questions this guideline answered on surrogate grounds. A reader can treat the post-prostatectomy recommendations as pointing the right way, but should not read the evidence grading as reflecting that later work. The tracer list is also dated: choline and 18F-NaF sit beside PSMA as alternatives, a menu a current reader would not treat as interchangeable.

Recommendation 4.7 matters more than its moderate strength suggests. It says NGI in hormone-sensitive metastatic disease could shift intent from multimodality management of oligometastatic disease to systemic therapy alone. That is stage migration with a treatment consequence. A pt who is oligometastatic on conventional imaging may be polymetastatic on PSMA, and metastasis-directed therapy evidence selected on conventional imaging then becomes harder to map onto the pt in front of you. The guideline names this risk without resolving it and cites limited prospective data.

What would make the framework wrong: if NGI-detected low-volume disease behaves like the micrometastatic disease conventional imaging always missed, then upstaging can withhold curative-intent salvage from men who would have benefited. The castration-resistant recommendations (4.8, 4.10) leave that open. They defer NGI to trials, or to cases where a change in care is already contemplated, which is the honest position on the data the panel had.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 4.4 is the RT-facing recommendation, and the only one graded high quality and strong: NGI before contemplated salvage RT after RP. Habl reported a changed RT plan in 59% after 68Ga-PSMA PET/CT, so field design is what NGI changes here.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: In hormone-sensitive metastatic disease, 4.7 allows NGI to shift intent from oligometastatic multimodality management to systemic therapy alone, on limited prospective data. In mCRPC, PSA progression alone should not change therapy (4.9), and NGI after radiographic progression is not routine (4.11).

sites.intro: Two reference documents: ABS HDR fractionation and dose goals, plus ESGO/ESTRO/ESP molecular testing and Lynch surveillance (its RT recommendations not in source excerpt).

studies.name: ESGO/ESTRO/ESP endometrial carcinoma guidelines
studies.tldr: ~3% of endometrial carcinomas are Lynch-related; the guideline advises MMR IHC or MSI testing in all EC regardless of histology (III, B) and four-test molecular classification.
details: 🔍 Joint ESGO/ESTRO/ESP update of the 2014 European consensus conference
🔍 Evidence base: systematic MEDLINE review, Jan 2014 to Jun 2019, English only
🔍 Grading: adapted IDSA-USPHS system, evidence levels I-V × grades A-E
🔍 191 external reviewers scored relevance and feasibility; patients reviewed qualitatively

details.text: 🧭 Graded recommendations captured in the source excerpt

rows: Multidisciplinary tumor board planning of staging + treatment
Treatment in a specialized gyn-onc center, esp. high-risk/advanced
MMR IHC (+ MLH1 promoter methylation if MLH1/PMS2 loss) or MSI in all EC, any histotype
Genetic counseling for EC pts at increased Lynch risk
Lynch EC surveillance generally from age 35, tailored to mutation + family history
Annual TVUS + annual or biennial endometrial biopsy until hysterectomy
Hysterectomy + BSO at completion of childbearing, preferably before age 40

details.text: 📊 Lynch cumulative cancer incidence at 70 years by mutated gene
🔗 Gene-specific surveillance start ages cited (Ryan et al)
subdetails: MSH6 and truncating MLH1: from age 40
Heterozygous PMS2: gynecological surveillance not warranted

details: 📊 Occult malignancy at prophylactic surgery in Lynch/HNPCC up to 17% (retrospective, Lachiewicz et al)
🔍 Molecular classification needs all four tests: p53, MSH6, PMS2 IHC + POLE exonuclease-domain sequencing
⚠️ Single surrogate test insufficient: multiple classifiers occur in ~5% of carcinomas
⚠️ Source excerpt truncated before adjuvant treatment section; RT recommendations not captured
studies.significance: The molecular classification that adjuvant decisions now lean on is valid only when all four tests are run: ~5% of carcinomas are multiple classifiers, and POLEmut requires a pathogenic exonuclease-domain variant. The guideline's adjuvant RT allocations fall past the truncation point of this excerpt, so the excerpt does not show which RT decision each molecular group moves.
studies.monday_clinic: In a Lynch syndrome mutation carrier, this supports hysterectomy plus BSO at completion of childbearing, preferably before 40, with counseling on occult cancer at surgery; it does not extend gynecological surveillance to heterozygous PMS2 carriers.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Joint ESGO/ESTRO/ESP guideline updating the **2014 European consensus conference**. Systematic MEDLINE review of studies published **Jan 2014 to Jun 2019**, English only, with priority to systematic reviews, meta-analyses and RCTs. Recommendations graded by an adapted IDSA-USPHS system (levels I-V, grades A-E), then scored by **191 external reviewers** with patient input.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Women with endometrial carcinoma across risk groups and histotypes, plus **Lynch syndrome mutation carriers** for surveillance and risk-reducing surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **MMR IHC or MSI in all endometrial carcinomas**, irrespective of histotype (III, B), with MLH1 promoter methylation analysis after MLH1/PMS2 loss. Molecular classification requires **p53, MSH6, PMS2 and POLE together**; POLEmut only with a pathogenic exonuclease-domain variant.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Aligns with ISGyP, which recommends MMR/MSI testing in all endometrial carcinomas irrespective of age, and with the Manchester International Consensus Group. Builds the surrogate classifier on the TCGA molecular groups, citing consistent prognostic relevance in independent cohorts and prospective trials.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents women with endometrial carcinoma of any histotype and Lynch syndrome mutation carriers. Does not represent adjuvant RT or systemic allocation by risk group, which falls outside the captured excerpt.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Single-database, **English-only** search closing **Jun 2019**, so later evidence is not graded here. Lynch surveillance and surgical-timing items rest on **retrospective (IV)** evidence, and the 17% occult-malignancy figure comes from a single retrospective series.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The operational change is that pathology now carries the risk stratification: a four-test panel replaces histology-only grouping, with an explicit rule against running one surrogate in isolation. L1CAM and CTNNB1 remain open candidates for refining low-grade NSMP disease.

studies.interpretation:
The most consequential move in this guideline is structural rather than therapeutic: it puts the TCGA-derived molecular classification into routine diagnostic workup and insists on the full panel. Requiring p53, MSH6 and PMS2 immunohistochemistry together with POLE exonuclease-domain sequencing, and refusing to let any one surrogate stand alone, is a quality rule as much as a biological one. The stated reason is that a combination of positive tests occurs in about 5% of carcinomas, so a lab running p53 alone would misassign a POLE-mutated or MMR-deficient tumor that also carries an abnormal p53 pattern. For anyone who uses molecular group to calibrate adjuvant intensity, the input is only as good as the panel, and this guideline makes incomplete testing a deviation rather than a shortcut.

On universal MMR testing the document follows ISGyP and the Manchester group rather than leading them. Its own contribution is to tie the test to four separate uses: diagnostic, Lynch pre-screening, prognostic, and predictive for checkpoint inhibitor benefit. That combination is what justifies testing every tumor regardless of age or histotype. Grading the recommendation III, B is honest about the evidence: the case for universal testing rests on cohort data and cost reasoning, not on randomized comparison.

The Lynch surveillance and risk-reducing surgery recommendations deserve more caution than their confident wording implies. All are graded IV, B. The gene-specific incidence figures make a reasonable case for tailoring, with endometrial risk at 70 years ranging from 24% for PMS2 to 51% for MSH2, and the cited Ryan et al ages track that gradient. Yet the formal recommendation settles on a general start age of 35 with individual adjustment, a compromise between a gene-specific schedule and a simple one. The 17% occult-malignancy ceiling at prophylactic surgery comes from one retrospective series and is best read as an upper bound for counseling, not a prevalence estimate.

The methodology limits what the document can settle. The literature search covers MEDLINE only, in English, and closes in June 2019, so it cannot grade molecularly directed adjuvant data published after that point. Its authority comes from the breadth of the development panel and the 191-reviewer external round, which measures acceptability and feasibility rather than outcome. That is the right tool for a consensus document, but a reader should treat its grades as a snapshot of 2019 evidence.

For the radiation oncologist, the captured excerpt stops just as the guideline turns to adjuvant treatment, so the risk-group allocations that move EBRT or vaginal brachytherapy decisions are not visible here. What the excerpt does fix is the upstream rule: whatever adjuvant allocation follows, it presumes the full four-test classification has been done.

significance_by_specialty.medonc: MMR status is framed as predictive for checkpoint inhibitor utility as well as a Lynch pre-screen, which is part of why the guideline advises MMR IHC or MSI in every endometrial carcinoma (III, B). The four-test molecular panel is the required basis for classification, with no single surrogate accepted.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Hysterectomy plus BSO in Lynch carriers is advised at completion of childbearing and preferably before age 40 (IV, B), with estrogen replacement after premenopausal BSO. Counseling should cover occult malignancy found at prophylactic surgery, reported up to 17% in one retrospective series.

studies.significance: Point A schedules are now only a starting point. The working goal is HR-CTV D90 85-95 Gy EQD2(10) from EMBRACE, and the EMBRACE-derived limits (rectum D2cc ≤65 Gy, bladder ≤80 Gy) are tighter than the ABS 70-75 / 80-90 Gy. The cited complication signal above 7 Gy/fx limits how freely 3 x 8 or 2 x 9 Gy should be used.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: ABS Gynecologic Cancer Task Force **compendium**. Members reviewed the literature and prior ABS consensus, discussed it on conference calls and added their own clinical experience. Recommendations were made **where there was agreement**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: HDR schedules are given for **intact cervix** (Point A and image-guided), **postop endometrial cuff** (alone or after EBRT), **vaginal recurrence**, **medically inoperable stage I uterine** disease, and **vaginal and cervical interstitial** brachy. The paired EQD2 values are there so isoeffective schedules can be estimated.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The cervix target follows **EMBRACE** (HR-CTV D90 **85-95 Gy EQD2(10)**). EMBRACE also supplies the lower rectal and bladder D2cc limits. The cuff section rests on the **Sorbe** randomized trial and on institutional series, including Portec-2.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents gyn pts receiving HDR brachytherapy with definitive, neoadjuvant or adjuvant intent for cervix, endometrial or vaginal disease. Does not represent dose-painting target volumes beyond HR-CTV, which the compendium leaves out.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The only randomized cuff evidence is the Sorbe trial in low-risk disease. The older ABS OAR limits are printed **alongside** the lower EMBRACE values without being reconciled. No search strategy or evidence grading is described.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Its main use is a conversion reference: it puts schedules prescribed to Point A, 0.5 cm depth, the vaginal surface or CTV on one EQD2 scale. It does not settle whether schedules matched on EQD2 differ in control or late toxicity. The authors concede that few data show one schedule beating another.

studies.interpretation:
This document is a reference table set, not an evidence synthesis, and should be read that way. The task force assembled it from earlier ABS consensus statements, the literature and its members' practice, through conference-call discussion. It describes no search strategy, no evidence grading and no formal voting. Its value is that it puts schedules usually quoted in incompatible units (Point A dose, 0.5 cm depth, vaginal surface, CTV) side by side with EQD2 conversions. It does not rank them. For the postoperative cuff the authors decline to recommend any regimen over another.

For intact cervix, the bigger change is that Point A is demoted. The Point A schedules are offered as an unoptimized starting point, and the actual goal is an HR-CTV D90 of 85-95 Gy EQD2(10) taken from EMBRACE, with the upper end for larger tumors at the time of brachytherapy. That brings the ABS reference in line with image-guided practice. Yet the older ABS organ limits (rectum and sigmoid D2cc 70-75 Gy, bladder 80-90 Gy) still sit next to the lower EMBRACE-derived values (rectum ≤65 Gy, bladder ≤80 Gy). A planner working from the ABS numbers alone accepts more rectal dose than the cohort that set the target goal. Reaching that goal took hybrid intracavitary/interstitial technique in about 45% of pts in the Vienna experience. That is a statement about resources as much as about dose.

The evidence is thinnest, and the toxicity stakes highest, in the section on fraction size. The text cites a complication signal above 7 Gy per fraction and a former ABS ceiling of 7.5 Gy/fx with at least four fractions. It still lists 3 x 8 Gy as acceptable, based on one trial that reported equivalent tumor and OAR outcomes against a four-fraction 6 Gy/fx regimen. It also allows 2 x 9 Gy for resource-poor settings, even though an international trial showed better local control with 4 x 7 Gy. These are practical concessions, not claims of equivalence. Tumor-side EQD2 arithmetic will not capture the late-effect cost of the larger fractions.

The postoperative endometrial section rests on one randomized comparison: Sorbe's 290-patient trial of 2.5 vs 5.0 Gy x 6 prescribed to 0.5 cm depth. Outcomes were equal, with more vaginal shortening at the higher dose. The trial enrolled only low-risk stage IA grade 1-2 disease, and its high-dose arm is above what is now accepted at 5 mm depth. Every other cuff schedule in the document is institutional. The practical point most likely to be missed is the cylinder-diameter caveat: a depth prescription built for a 3 cm cylinder has to be modified on a 2.5 cm cylinder to keep the surface dose comparable.

The compendium leaves open whether schedules matched on EQD2 actually perform alike for local control and late vaginal, rectal and bladder toxicity. It does not try to answer that question.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Point A schedules are now only a starting point. The working goal is HR-CTV D90 85-95 Gy EQD2(10) from EMBRACE, and the EMBRACE-derived limits (rectum D2cc ≤65 Gy, bladder ≤80 Gy) are tighter than the ABS 70-75 / 80-90 Gy. The cited complication signal above 7 Gy/fx limits how freely 3 x 8 or 2 x 9 Gy should be used.

papers.abstract: PURPOSE Provide evidence- and expert-based recommendations for optimal use of imaging in advanced prostate cancer. Due to increases in research and utilization of novel imaging for advanced prostate cancer, this guideline is intended to outline techniques available and provide recommendations on appropriate use of imaging for specified patient subgroups. METHODS An Expert Panel was convened with members from ASCO and the Society of Abdominal Radiology, American College of Radiology, Society of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, American Urological Association, American Society for Radiation Oncology, and Society of Urologic Oncology to conduct a systematic review of the literature and develop an evidence-based guideline on the optimal use of imaging for advanced prostate cancer. Representative index cases of various prostate cancer disease states are presented, including suspected high-risk disease, newly diagnosed treatment-naïve metastatic disease, suspected recurrent disease after local treatment, and progressive disease while undergoing systemic treatment. A systematic review of the literature from 2013 to August 2018 identified fully published English-language systematic reviews with or without meta-analyses, reports of rigorously conducted phase III randomized controlled trials that compared ≥ 2 imaging modalities, and noncomparative studies that reported on the efficacy of a single imaging modality. RESULTS A total of 35 studies met inclusion criteria and form the evidence base, including 17 systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis and 18 primary research articles. RECOMMENDATIONS One or more of these imaging modalities should be used for patients with advanced prostate cancer: conventional imaging (defined as computed tomography [CT], bone scan, and/or prostate magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]) and/or next-generation imaging (NGI), positron emission tomography [PET], PET/CT, PET/MRI, or whole-body MRI) according to the clinical scenario.
